summary: The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) provides access to routing information bases. This document updates BMP (RFC 7854) by adding access to the Local RIB (Loc-RIB), the table of routes a BGP speaker has selected through its Decision Process, as defined in RFC 4271.

plainLanguage.summary: A router keeps a list of its chosen best routes. This document lets monitoring tools peek at that list too, not just the routes the router heard from others.

questions: how to monitor bgp local rib
how does bmp monitor the bgp loc-rib

subtitle: How a router can show a BMP monitoring station the routes it actually selected, not just the routes it heard.

tldr.problem: BMP could export what a router received from its peers, but not the router's own table of selected routes (the Loc-RIB). Monitoring tools had to rebuild that table from raw inputs, or from another router's view.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a Loc-RIB Instance Peer type (3) to BMP. The router acts as an emulated peer, sending Peer Up and Down messages plus Route Monitoring messages that carry its Loc-RIB.
tldr.outcome: A monitoring system can read the selected routes directly, per VRF or table, without extra BGP peering. The RFC updates RFC 7854, and RFC 9736 later updates this one.

today: RFC 9069 is a Proposed Standard from February 2022 that updates RFC 7854. It has not been obsoleted, but it is itself updated by RFC 9736.

sections.title: Why Monitor the Loc-RIB
sections.content:
The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP, RFC 7854) exports BGP routing data to monitoring stations. It had no way to send a BGP instance's Loc-RIB: the routes the local speaker selected through its Decision Process, which include selected routes from peers and locally originated routes. This document adds that and replaces Section 8.2 of RFC 7854 ('Locally Originated Routes').

It gives three use cases. First, a tool that only needs the selected routes should not have to ingest every post-policy Adj-RIB-In, which may hold hundreds of thousands of routes, and redo the best-path selection. Second, a history of Loc-RIB changes helps troubleshooting, for example a problem that lasted only 5 minutes. Third, operators can compare Adj-RIB-In post-policy with the Loc-RIB to validate that policy and multipath installed what was expected.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of making a detective read every letter the router received, you just show them the short list of roads the router actually decided to use.

sections.title: The Indirect Alternative
sections.content:
Without this feature, you can infer a router's Loc-RIB by peering a second router with it and monitoring that second router's pre-policy Adj-RIB-In. The RFC calls this complex and error prone.

It needs at least two routers when only one was to be monitored, and extra BGP peering that may not otherwise exist (the RFC names VRF tables with no peers as an example). The outbound policy on the peering may also generate aggregates, suppress prefixes, change attributes or filter routes, so the view no longer matches the real Loc-RIB. Finally, BGP peering carries no internal system information such as the router name, so the monitoring side must correlate BGP identifiers and addresses using data it gets from outside BMP.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way is asking a neighbor what the router told them. The neighbor may have left things out, so the answer is only a guess.

sections.title: Peer Type and Per-Peer Header
sections.content:
A new peer type, 3, is the Loc-RIB Instance Peer. Locally sourced routes sent through BMP MUST use it. Its only defined peer flag is F, which MUST be set when a filter limits what Loc-RIB routes go to the BMP collector. Other bits are reserved: sent as 0 and ignored on receipt.

In the per-peer header of all messages for this peer type, the Peer Distinguisher is zero for the global instance (otherwise the route distinguisher or a unique local value), and the Peer Address is zero-filled. The Peer AS is the router's primary ASN, and the Peer BGP ID is the router-id of the VRF instance, or the global router-id. The Timestamp is when the routes were installed in the Loc-RIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The watcher needs a name tag for this special 'peer', so the router uses a new tag type and fills in the details that make sense, leaving the rest as zeros.

sections.title: How Loc-RIB Monitoring Works
sections.content:
The router emulates a peer. A Peer Up notification follows RFC 7854 with these clarifications: local address, local port and remote port are zero, and the Sent OPEN message is fabricated. It MUST include the 4-octet ASN capability and the capabilities needed to represent Loc-RIB messages. The Received OPEN is a repeat of the sent one.

A new Peer Up information TLV, type 3, is the VRF/Table Name, a UTF-8 string of 1 to 255 bytes. If a name is configured it MUST be included, and the default name global is used for the default Loc-RIB instance. The Peer Down notification uses reason code 6 and repeats the name TLV if it was in the Peer Up.

Route Monitoring messages do the initial synchronization and then carry incremental changes, using 4-byte ASN encoding. Senders SHOULD use state compression and throttling, so that, for example, five changes to one prefix within a second may be sent as just the final one. Route Mirroring does not apply, and received mirroring messages SHOULD be ignored. For Statistics Reports, Stat Type 8 gives the number of routes in Loc-RIB and Stat Type 10 gives the number per AFI/SAFI.
sections.plainLanguage: The router pretends to be a little neighbor that hands the watcher its best-roads list, sends updates when the list changes, and can skip sending tiny changes that were quickly undone.

sections.title: Multiple Instances, Filtering and Changes
sections.content:
There MUST be at least one emulated peer for each Loc-RIB instance, such as each VRF. The receiver identifies a Loc-RIB by the peer distinguisher and BGP ID, and uses the VRF/Table Name for a label. If more than one emulated peer is needed to carry different address families for one Loc-RIB, they share the distinguisher and BGP ID, and each sends its own Peer Up with its address family capabilities.

The router may filter what it exports, for example sending only EBGP routes and not IBGP or IGP ones. When it does, the F flag is set to 1, and if several filters apply to the same Loc-RIB a table name MUST be used so the receiver can tell them apart. If filtering or table names change on an existing BMP session, the session MUST be bounced with a Peer Down and Peer Up sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: Each separate routing table gets its own stand-in neighbor. If the router hides some roads from the watcher, it raises a flag so the watcher knows the list is partial.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations in Section 11 of RFC 7854 apply. Implementations SHOULD only establish sessions with authorized and trusted monitoring devices, and the RFC believes it adds no further security considerations.

IANA registered peer type 3 (Loc-RIB Instance Peer), created a registry for Loc-RIB Instance Peer flags with flag 0 as F and flags 1 to 7 unassigned, registered Peer Up Information TLV type 3 (VRF/Table Name) and Peer Down reason code 6. It also marked the old F flag in the registry for peer types 0 through 2 as deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: Only let trusted watchers listen in, because the router's route list is private.
